input.question: Is it possible that Mercury is the remnant core of a gas giant destroyed in a past supernova?
input.ground_truth: Any supernova close enough to rip mercury to shreds would have left a lot of evidence here on Earth which we do not see. We do have some subtle evidence of supernovae going off in the same neck of the woods as the sun some 10s of millions of years ago, but nothing that would impact the bulk properties of a planet nearby.

Okay! Imagine you have a big, fluffy cake (that’s like a gas giant planet). Sometimes, if something very, very big and powerful (like a supernova, which is a giant explosion in space) happens, the cake might get blown apart! All the fluffy part (the gas) goes away, but sometimes a little hard piece in the middle (the core) can stay behind.

Some people wonder if Mercury, which is a small, rocky planet close to the Sun, is actually that leftover hard piece from a much bigger planet that got blown up long ago by a big space explosion. But scientists don’t have proof of that yet. It’s just a fun idea!

So, the answer is: Maybe, but we don’t know for sure. It’s like guessing if a tiny rock you found is from a cake that exploded long ago!
